system_overview: This specification models the Dijkstra-Scholten algorithm for detecting termination of diffusing computations in a distributed system. The algorithm was published by E.W. Dijkstra and C.S. Scholten in 'Termination detection for diffusing computations' (Information Processing Letters, 11(1):1-4, 1980). The algorithm detects when a distributed computation initiated by a single leader process has terminated, meaning all processes are idle and no messages are in transit. The key insight is constructing a dynamic overlay tree over an arbitrary network topology, where non-neutral processes form a tree rooted at the leader.
actors_and_components: The system consists of a set of processes connected by a directed graph (network). One distinguished process is the leader, which initiates the computation. The leader has only outgoing edges and cannot receive computation messages. Each process can be either busy (computing) or idle. Busy processes can send computation messages along outgoing edges. The algorithm introduces control messages called acknowledgments (acks) that flow in the reverse direction of computation messages. An overlay tree is dynamically maintained, where each non-neutral process has a parent in the tree.
state_variables: The system tracks: (1) whether each process is currently active (busy) or idle, (2) for each directed edge, the count of messages sent along that edge that have not yet been acknowledged, (3) for each directed edge, the count of messages received along that edge that have not yet been acknowledged by the receiver, (4) for each non-leader process, which edge connects it to its parent in the overlay tree (or a sentinel value indicating the process has no parent), (5) for each edge, the number of computation messages currently in transit, and (6) for each edge, the number of acknowledgment (control) messages currently in transit.
initial_state: Initially, only the leader is active (busy); all other processes are idle. No computation messages have been sent, so all message and acknowledgment counters on all edges are zero. No non-leader process has a parent in the overlay tree.
actions: The algorithm defines five types of actions: (1) Send message: an active process sends a computation message along one of its outgoing edges, incrementing the sent-unacknowledged counter and the in-transit message count for that edge. (2) Receive acknowledgment: a process receives an acknowledgment on one of its outgoing edges, decrementing both the ack-in-transit counter and the sent-unacknowledged counter. (3) Send acknowledgment: a process sends an acknowledgment back along an incoming edge, subject to constraints that prevent the process from sending its last ack to its parent until the process is neutral (idle, with all messages acknowledged in both directions). When a process becomes neutral after sending an ack, it removes itself from the overlay tree. (4) Receive message: a process receives a computation message on an incoming edge, becoming active. If the process was neutral before receiving, the sender becomes the process's parent in the overlay tree. (5) Idle: an active process may become idle at any time.
safety_properties: The main safety property is that if the leader is neutral (idle, with all sent messages acknowledged and all received messages acknowledged), then every other process is also neutral. This ensures the leader detects termination only when the computation has truly terminated. Additionally, the overlay tree of non-neutral processes always forms a valid tree rooted at the leader (when non-empty), and the message counters remain consistent: for any edge, the sent-unacknowledged count equals the sum of received-unacknowledged count, in-transit acks, and in-transit messages.
liveness_properties: If the computation terminates (all processes become idle and there are no messages in transit), then the leader eventually becomes neutral, thereby detecting termination.
model_bounds: The set of processes and the network topology (directed edge set) are declared as constants. For model checking, these must be instantiated with specific finite sets. Message and acknowledgment counters may need explicit bounds to keep the state space finite.
additional_assumptions: Messages are never lost (both computation and control messages are delivered reliably). Message ordering does not matter for correctness. Self-loops are not allowed in the network graph. Non-Byzantine process failures cannot cause the leader to falsely believe a non-terminated computation has terminated, but may prevent termination from being detected. Weak fairness is assumed for the next-state action.
